First, trajectory reconstruction. The model is treated as a flow-matching or ODE-based generator with a learned velocity field. Given a real video encoded into the pretrained VAE latent space, the authors integrate the velocity field backward from the clean latent toward noise, producing an approximate reverse trajectory. This allows them to rerun the backbone at each time step and collect block-level hidden states and attention patterns. The appendix discusses approximation error and the conditions under which the recovered trajectory is a faithful proxy. Second, linear probing. They train lightweight probes on intermediate transformer states to predict physical plausibility and some quantitative physical variables. The point is not to maximize probe capacity, but to localize where and when physical information becomes linearly accessible. Third, causal intervention. They perform block-level noise interventions and use a probe-surprise style analysis to identify which components carry or amplify the physical signal. This goes beyond standard probing: it asks not only whether the information is readable, but also whether perturbing specific computations changes the signal and downstream generation. Compared with predictive representation learners such as V-JEPA, the model here is not trained with an explicit future-prediction objective. Compared with standard diffusion interpretability work, the analysis is anchored on real videos embedded back into the model’s trajectory rather than on arbitrary generated samples.bc:T56d,The experiments are organized around a few core phenomena rather than a broad benchmark sweep. First, on real videos with known physical plausibility labels, the recovered trajectories show that physical plausibility is linearly decodable from intermediate diffusion-transformer states. The signal is not uniform across the network: it tends to peak at certain depths and noise levels, often in intermediate blocks rather than at the input latent or final layer. Second, the paper reports that some quantitative physical variables are also decodable, which suggests the model is not merely storing a coarse plausible-versus-implausible cue. Third, the strength of the signal depends on trajectory fidelity: when the reconstructed path better follows the model’s learned continuous dynamics, probe performance improves, supporting the claim that physical structure emerges from denoising dynamics. Fourth, intervention experiments show that perturbing specific blocks weakens decodability or changes generation behavior, indicating that these layers are involved in forming and transmitting the signal rather than passively correlating with it. The provided text does not include the full numeric tables, model sizes, or training-scale details, but the study is clearly conducted on modern video diffusion transformers operating in a pretrained VAE latent space rather than on toy models.bd:T768,The method section has two parts. First, the paper validates the mechanism. In prefix-perturbation experiments, the authors modify only the template prefix before the user query, sometimes with very small changes such as capitalization, while keeping the query semantics intact. Alignment is often restored. In contrast, if the prefix is kept unchanged, replacing the user query with similar or even random tokens can still preserve the misaligned behavior. This suggests that the trigger is concentrated in the shared prefix rather than in the semantic content of the query.

They then move from correlational evidence to a stronger causal intervention using representation patching. Specifically, they replace the KV-cache entries at prefix positions in the finetuned misaligned model with the corresponding entries from the original unfrozen? no, original frozen pre-finetuning model, across all layers. This leaves the query untouched but forces the information propagated from prefix positions to revert to its pre-finetuning state. The intervention largely restores alignment, indicating that prefix representations indeed encode the harmful behavioral bias.

Second, they introduce TReFT, Token-Regularized Finetuning. Instead of relying on retain-set interleaving, TReFT regularizes selected token representations so that shared prefix tokens do not drift too far from the base model, while allowing more of the update to land on tokens that encode the actual query content. The design choice is important: standard output supervision tells the model what behavior to produce, but not which context should scope that behavior. TReFT adds an inductive bias over attribution, pushing the model to associate new behavior with domain semantics rather than with globally shared template tokens. The paper also applies the same idea beyond EM to abstention, tool calling, and refusal behaviors.be:T44f,Three result groups matter most. First, the prefix brittleness experiments show that tiny perturbations to the chat-template prefix can sharply reduce emergent misalignment without changing the query semantics. That is the main behavioral evidence for piggybacking. Second, the KV-cache patching experiment provides the strongest causal result: on Llama-3.1-8B, patching prefix representations from the unfinetuned model raises the alignment score from 40.8 to 90.4. This is a large recovery and suggests the issue is encoded in internal prefix representations rather than only in output-layer drift. Third, TReFT consistently mitigates OOD misgeneralization while preserving the intended in-domain behavior. The headline number in the paper is that on Llama-3.1-7B in the legal-domain setting, TReFT reduces EM 33.5% better than data interleaving. The utility-preservation result is also important, because many mitigation methods work by simply weakening the learned behavior overall.bf:T99e,There is no new model or training recipe here, but the argument is structured carefully. The paper starts by criticizing the “fix it in post” mindset: when undesirable behavior appears, the default response is finetuning, RLHF, or input/output filtering, rather than asking how the behavior was produced during pretraining or intermediate training. The authors use examples such as brittle safety finetuning and superficial bias mitigation to argue that post-hoc interventions often change outputs without addressing the underlying causal mechanism.

The paper then borrows from Kuhn’s criteria for scientific theories and asks what a science of AI should look like. The answer is not just better benchmark optimization. A scientific account should support empirical prediction, internal consistency across optimization/data/architecture/representation changes, compatibility with adjacent theory, broad scope beyond one benchmark, simplicity where possible, and the ability to generate new experiments.

The most actionable part is the three-level agenda around training dynamics. First is prediction: using early training signals to forecast later capabilities, failure modes, and alignment properties, not only final loss. This points toward studying gradient statistics, representation geometry, sample learning order, subdistribution absorption rates, and the timing of capability emergence. Second is intervention: if a trajectory is going wrong, one should be able to steer it through data mixture changes, sampling schedules, optimizer settings, regularization, or stage transitions. Third is design: replacing large amounts of trial-and-error with training procedures that are intentionally constructed to yield target properties.

Methodologically, the paper argues for longitudinal measurement rather than endpoint-only evaluation. That means linking checkpoints, internal states, behavior, and exposure history across training time. This stands in contrast to much of mechanistic interpretability, which often studies final models, and much of alignment work, which often studies post-trained behavior without tracing its developmental origin. The paper implicitly calls for stronger experimental design as well: controlled data-mixture studies, repeated runs to estimate trajectory variance, sample-level learning event logging, and tests of whether post-training actually changes internal representations rather than only decision boundaries.c0:T464,The technical strategy is a unified framework supported by mathematical appendices and instantiated across multiple modalities. The text appears to start from intelligence, memory, prediction, and compression, then builds the machinery through optimization, automatic differentiation, entropy, diffusion, denoising, and rate-distortion theory. It then applies the framework to image autoencoding and sampling, text-conditioned image generation, video extension, 3D tokenization and generation, motion generation, natural language modeling, and white-box transformer variants. For language, the key implementation seems to be a model called Causal CRATE, together with sections on optimization strategy, evaluation methodology, width scaling, linear-time transformers, and attention-only variants. The novelty is not a single algorithmic trick. Exact metrics and numeric deltas are likely in the Results/Appendix sections not included in the excerpt.c3:T43c,Pipeline: empirical symptom → interpretability tools → subspace identification → linear filtering.
1) Symptom via Logit Lens: projecting raw text embeddings through the unembedding matrix yields top vocabulary probabilities dominated by high-frequency tokens across model families.
2) Hypothesis: embedding anisotropy concentrates representations around a frequency-weighted centroid (“average token”), suppressing semantic variation.
3) Subspace discovery via Logit Spectroscopy: analyzing a reverse-engineered average-token representation reveals an “edge spectrum” subspace spanned by right singular vectors at both ends of the unembedding matrix’s singular value spectrum (largest and smallest singular values).
4) Fix: EmbedFilter, a simple linear transformation that truncates/removes embedding components in this edge-spectrum subspace. It is constructed from existing unembedding parameters and requires no training.
5) Claimed side benefit: approximately distance-preserving behavior enables dimensionality reduction for cheaper indexing and faster retrieval.c4:T803,The analysis uses a standard tractable testbed for ICL theory: a single-layer linear attention model trained on linear regression prompts. This choice is deliberate. Full transformers are too hard to analyze cleanly, while linear attention has been shown in prior work to reproduce several qualitative ICL phenomena. The paper’s main modeling contribution is the task distribution: instead of sampling task vectors from a single family, it samples them from a mixture of Gaussians, with each mixture component restricted to a low-dimensional subspace. These subspaces overlap through a shared common subspace.

This structure lets the authors study how gradient descent first aligns with the shared subspace and only later captures component-specific directions. The loss plateau is interpreted as the phase before the model has identified the common structure that is useful across tasks. Once that shared structure is learned, gradients from different task components reinforce each other, and optimization accelerates. In that sense, diversity helps not because tasks are arbitrarily different, but because multiple related tasks provide a stronger and more stable signal on the common latent structure.

For generalization, especially OOD, the paper argues that success depends on whether test tasks lie near the span or coverage induced by the training subspaces. If training tasks cover a richer set of structured directions while still sharing common components, the model can extrapolate better. If test tasks fall outside that structural support, diversity alone does not guarantee transfer. This is a useful distinction for pretraining: coverage matters, but structured coverage matters more.

Relative to earlier work, Kim et al. mainly provided empirical evidence that task diversity shortens the plateau, and Goddard et al. empirically linked diversity to OOD behavior under a different task definition. This paper’s novelty is the overlapping-subspace formulation that makes both effects analyzable within one mathematical framework.c5:T4bb,The experiments serve mainly to validate the theory and reproduce known qualitative phenomena rather than to establish a new benchmark. The paper reproduces the observation that training on a mixture of related task families converges faster than training on each family separately; the left panel of Figure 2 is highlighted as showing earlier escape from the plateau and faster approach to near-optimal performance under task diversity. It also varies the degree of subspace overlap, the number of mixture components, and the dimensions of shared versus private subspaces to show how these factors affect plateau length and OOD behavior.

The experimental setup stays within the linear-regression / linear-attention testbed. The main outputs are trends, not headline absolute numbers: stronger shared subspaces lead to larger optimization gains from joint training, and broader structured subspace coverage improves OOD generalization. The provided full-content excerpt does not include the complete result tables, so it would be unsafe to invent exact gains. What is clear is that the paper treats both optimization speed and OOD transfer as controlled variables tied to the geometry of the task distribution.c6:T44d,Read it as a mechanism paper. Instead, it builds an empirical case that an alternative explanation can account for alignment-faking-like behavior.

The first step is to challenge a simple prediction of the scheming story. If a model is pretending to be aligned during evaluation mainly to avoid weight modification, then explicitly telling it that it is already deployed should reduce that incentive or at least alter the behavior pattern. The authors report that evaluation awareness persists even under deployment-framed system prompts. They use this as evidence that a pure self-preservation account is incomplete.

The second step is to test whether sycophancy-related internal features can explain the same behaviors. They use activation probing and activation steering with features described as scheming-related and sycophancy-related, asking which features better account for the observed context-sensitive behavior. The argumentative structure is important: they are not proving that scheming is absent, but that sycophancy is a plausible competing mechanism with empirical support.

The third step is an intervention through fine-tuning. They make models more sycophantic and then measure whether evaluation-cue detection improves. The intended logic is that if increasing sycophancy also increases sensitivity to evaluation context, then evaluation awareness need not be uniquely explained by strategic deception or self-preservation.

Methodologically, this is a concept-clarification paper backed by probing, steering, prompt manipulation, and behavioral comparison. Its main contribution is to separate a behavioral label from an intent-level interpretation and to provide evidence for an alternative causal story.c8:T660,From the provided full text, three empirical claims stand out.

First, evaluation awareness persists even when models are told they are deployed. The authors treat this as evidence against a scheming-only explanation, because a model motivated purely by avoiding weight updates should have less reason to conceal itself under deployment framing. The strength of this result depends heavily on prompt construction, model choice, and the exact behavioral metric, so those details matter a lot.

Second, activation probing and steering suggest that sycophancy-related features can explain a substantial portion of behavior previously attributed to scheming. The excerpt does not include the full quantitative tables, so the direction of the result is visible but the effect size is not. A careful read should check how the features are labeled, what the probes are trained to predict, whether steering strengths are comparable, and whether scheming and sycophancy features are themselves highly correlated.

Third, fine-tuning for greater sycophancy appears to improve evaluation-cue detection. If robust, that would support a manipulable link between researcher-directed sycophancy and evaluation awareness. But the key question is whether the model becomes genuinely more situationally aware or merely more sensitive to superficial evaluation cues.

Overall, the experiments look more like evidence for an alternative causal interpretation than a decisive resolution of the debate. Without stronger cross-model robustness, larger-scale controls, and more explicit handling of confounders, the conclusions should be read with caution.c9:T4f6,This is a skim paper rather than a deep-read priority. For a pretraining-focused reader, this is best treated as a useful safety-interpretation note rather than a high-priority technical paper.ca:T9e3,方法上最关键的是数据构造和干预设计。作者不直接在自然文本里做相关性分析，而是利用“同一个词既可以被 tokenizer 表成单 token，也可以被人工拆成多个 subword”这一事实，构造 canonical form 与 artificial split form 的对照。然后定义 canonicity：比较 canonical 单 token 运行时该词位置的最终层 residual，与 split 运行时最后一个 subword 位置的最终层 residual 是否对齐。这个指标用来判断 split 后模型有没有在内部成功恢复出 canonical 词表示。

为了把 attention 与 MLP 的作用拆开，作者设计了两类配对样本。LST pair 共享最后一个 subword，不同的是前文子词；FST pair 共享第一个 subword，不同的是最后子词。这样可以分别隔离“跨位置传来的信息”和“本地末尾子词本身的贡献”。在这些配对上做 activation patching：把 source run 某层某位置的 attn_out 或 mlp_out 替换到 target run，再看 target 最终重建成哪个词。结果显示，在 Layer 1 的最后子词位置，patch attention 输出就足以把 target 的重建词拉向 source 的词，说明 attention 已经携带了决定性跨位置信号；而 patch MLP 输出则对应把这个信号与本地子词组合成更完整的词级表示。

论文提出的机制可以概括为：
1. 对于两到六个 subword 的词，真正发生组合的位置始终是最后一个 subword；
2. 如果词更长，中间 subword 位置主要充当 relay，把前面子词的信息逐步传到最后位置；
3. Layer 1 attention 负责传输 token-specific signal，这个信号较弱、线性可读，但已经足以决定后续会往哪个词收敛；
4. Layer 1 MLP 负责把该信号和末尾子词 embedding 做连续变换，得到更接近 canonical token 的表示；
5. 后续若干早层继续完成 detokenization，但关键起点已经在第一层建立。

作者还把分析扩展到 12 个 transformer LM，比较不同架构和位置编码。结论不是“所有模型都在同一层完成 detokenization”，而是 detokenization 集中在前 6% 到 30% 的层数区间，跨度主要由 positional encoding 决定。也就是说，位置编码如果更利于局部顺序信息在早层传播，detokenization 会更快完成；如果不利，则需要更多层。最后，作者在 activation patching 找到的关键深度上拟合一个线性方向，用早层激活预测最终 detokenization 成败，形成一个可操作的 probe。cb:T42f,The paper asks a precise mechanistic question: how do transformer LMs convert subword-fragmented input back into a usable word-level representation, and why does this process sometimes fail? Prior work had already suggested that detokenization happens in early-to-middle layers and involves both attention and MLPs, but the causal chain was still coarse. This work narrows it down substantially. Using controlled canonical-vs-split word pairs and activation patching, the authors show that English detokenization in Llama2-7B, and similarly in a broader set of transformer LMs, starts as a two-stage computation in Layer 1. A small set of attention heads first transmits a token-specific signal from earlier subwords to the final subword position; then the Layer 1 MLP combines that imported signal with the local subword representation to produce a continuous word-level representation. The paper also studies how this mechanism scales with word length, how it varies across architectures, and whether early-layer activations can predict eventual detokenization success.cc:T4df,This matters for pretraining research because it turns the tokenizer-model interface into something mechanistically inspectable rather than merely behaviorally observable. Tokenization artifacts are known to hurt robustness, arithmetic, and rare-token behavior, but this paper identifies where the model repairs the mismatch between subword input and word-level semantics. That is useful for thinking about tokenizer design, early-layer representation formation, and failure modes induced by poor segmentation. A second important result is that the depth over which detokenization unfolds is governed more by positional encoding than by model scale. That is a concrete architectural claim, not just an interpretability observation, and it suggests that early semantic composition depends on how positional information supports cross-token aggregation. Third, the paper provides a linear probe from early-layer activations that predicts final detokenization success with AUROC 0.94 on isolated inputs and 0.97 on natural text. That makes detokenization a measurable training signal. It could plausibly become a diagnostic for comparing tokenizers, monitoring training dynamics, or studying when word-level concepts become stable during pretraining.cd:Ta04,The core methodological contribution is the combination of a tightly controlled dataset construction with causal intervention. Instead of probing arbitrary natural text, the authors exploit words that can appear either as a single canonical token or as an artificially split sequence of subwords. They define a canonicity measure by comparing the final-layer residual stream at the canonical token position with the final-layer residual stream at the last subword position in the split run. High similarity means the model has successfully reconstructed the canonical word representation from fragments.

To separate the roles of attention and MLPs, they build paired examples with shared subwords. In one setup, pairs share the last subword but differ in earlier fragments, isolating the contribution of cross-position information. In another, pairs share the first subword but differ in the final fragment, isolating the contribution of the local final-subword identity. They then perform activation patching: replace attn_out or mlp_out from a source run into a target run at a specific layer and position, and observe which word the target ultimately reconstructs. This is the key causal move. In Layer 1 at the final subword position, patching attention output is already sufficient to redirect the target toward the source word, showing that attention carries the decisive imported signal. Patching the MLP output then shows how that signal is transformed together with the local final-subword representation into a more canonical word-level state.

The resulting mechanism is fairly crisp. For words split into two to six subwords, composition consistently happens at the last subword position. Intermediate positions mainly act as relays when the word is longer. Layer 1 attention transports a weak but linearly readable token-specific signal from earlier fragments. Layer 1 MLP composes that imported signal with the local subword embedding through a continuous transformation. Subsequent early layers continue the process, but the decisive initialization happens immediately.

The authors extend the analysis to 12 transformer LMs and compare architectures and positional encodings. Their claim is not that every model detokenizes in exactly one layer, but that detokenization is concentrated in the first 6% to 30% of layers, with the span largely determined by positional encoding. Finally, they fit a linear direction at the depth identified by patching and use it to predict whether detokenization will succeed, based only on early-layer activations.ce:T7c6,There are four experimental results worth retaining.

First, the mechanism localization result. In Llama2-7B, Layer 1 is already causally central. Patching Layer 1 attention output at the final subword position can change which word is reconstructed at the end of the network, while Layer 1 MLP output further sharpens that representation toward the canonical token. This supports a sequential division of labor: attention transports, MLP composes.

Second, the word-length generalization result. The authors test words split into 2 to 6 subwords and find that the final subword remains the composition site throughout. Longer words do not induce distributed semantic composition across all positions; instead, intermediate positions mostly relay information forward until the last position can assemble the word-level representation.

Third, the cross-model comparison. Across 12 transformer language models, detokenization is concentrated in the first 6% to 30% of layers. The important claim is that this depth tracks positional encoding more than parameter count. That weakens a simple scale-based explanation and points to an architectural determinant of early semantic aggregation.

Fourth, the predictability result. A linear probe trained on early-layer activations at the patching-identified depth predicts final detokenization success with AUROC around 0.94 on isolated contextless sequences and 0.97 on natural text. This suggests that success or failure is largely decided very early, and that the signal transfers beyond the synthetic split-word setup.

The paper also discusses failure cases where the imported early-layer signal is too weak or ambiguous, making later recovery incomplete. That aligns with known tokenization-related failures on undertrained tokens and difficult segmentations. When reading the full paper, it is worth checking the effect sizes for different patching conditions and the plots comparing detokenization depth across positional encoding schemes.cf:T722,Read it in four passes: definition, causal design, mechanism, and boundary conditions.

The authors study three high-redundancy MoE LMs: OLMoE-1B-7B-0924, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. These models span major MoE design choices: different load-balancing objectives, different top-k activation ratios, scratch training versus dense upcycling, and the presence or absence of shared experts. At five representative layers per model, they evaluate four standard observational metrics: utilization rate, activation norm, mean routing weight when active, and activation standard deviation. These are corpus-level expert summaries. They then compare them against token-level interventional effects using router-aware ablation. For an expert active at token t, they zero that expert’s output and measure the resulting next-token loss change, ΔL_i^(t), as the functional-importance target. They also report residual-stream displacement, the gap norm, as a representation-level effect size. To rule out lack of statistical power, they add a stronger control: instead of using population-averaged routing summaries, they use the token-conditioned routing weight g_i(x_t) itself. This gives routing-derived signals their best possible chance. The key design choice is that the comparison is made on the same token, layer, and active-expert event, so the paper is genuinely testing whether observational rankings predict interventional consequences.d1:T466,The main result is a strong null. Across 60 metric-layer combinations—four observational metrics, five layers, three models—none reaches Bonferroni-corrected significance. Effect sizes remain small throughout, with Cohen’s d below 0.17, and even the sign is not stable across layers. In other words, standard observational metrics have essentially no predictive value for token-level expert ablation effects in these models. The routing-weight control shows this is not a power issue: under the same machinery and sample size, token-conditioned routing weight recovers one Bonferroni-significant effect. The provided excerpt truncates later parts of the results (e.g., details of acoustic probes and additional quantitative metrics).d6:T641,The method has three stages. First, the authors define two pooled representations for each query q. The input embedding e_in(q) is obtained by running the prompt once and mean-pooling the final-layer hidden states over the prompt tokens. The thinking embedding e_th(q) is obtained by generating a reasoning trace and mean-pooling the final-layer hidden states over the <think>...</think> span. Second, they analyze the geometry of these two sets. Across models and benchmarks, both sets show extreme conicity: vectors cluster tightly around a single mean direction. However, the mean input direction mu_in and the mean thinking direction mu_th are not aligned; the paper reports an average cosine of about 0.66 across tested settings, while within-space alignment is much closer to 1. This combination of near-one-dimensional structure plus cross-space misalignment motivates an orthogonal mapping. Third, they fit an orthogonal Procrustes transform R on a small set of correctly solved examples, minimizing the discrepancy between R e_in and e_th. At inference time, they compute e_in for a new query, form a synthetic thinking vector e_hat_th = R e_in, and inject it as a single embedding position between <think> and </think> through the inputs_embeds interface. Two design choices matter here. They restrict the map to be orthogonal rather than affine or nonlinear, which keeps the hypothesis sharp and avoids hiding capacity in an adapter. And they fit R on held-out solved examples rather than target-benchmark data, aiming to capture model geometry rather than task-specific prompting patterns.d7:T521,The study spans four model families, roughly 4B to 31B parameters, and benchmarks in math, science, and code reasoning. On the geometry side, the fitted rotation reconstructs thinking embeddings with cosine similarity above 0.96 and mean squared error below 0.05 across tested settings, which is strong evidence that the prompt-to-thinking transition is well approximated by a single matrix. On downstream accuracy, Rotate2Think improves 30 out of 32 model-benchmark combinations, indicating that the effect is not confined to one architecture or one task family. The most striking transfer result is cross-modal: a rotation fitted only on text reasoning transfers zero-shot to visual math reasoning on MATH-Vision (testmini). For Gemma-4 E4B, Base+R2T reaches 38.1%, exceeding the model’s full reasoning-mode accuracy of 34.9% on a modality never seen during fitting. That result supports the claim that the learned transform reflects a model-internal reasoning geometry rather than a dataset-specific textual template. For deeper follow-up, the most interesting open questions are why final-layer mean pooling is sufficient, and whether this kind of rotation could be encouraged during pretraining or mid-training as an explicit reasoning-state regularizer.d9:T505,The proposed framework is GLU, for Global-Local Uncertainty. The local component is a standard token-level uncertainty measure, with the paper comparing Shannon entropy and evidential epistemic entropy variants under length normalization. The global component is built from the hidden-state trajectory during generation. For a response of length T, the model collects hidden states into a T by d matrix H, forms the Gram matrix K = H H^T, and computes a matrix Rényi entropy from the eigenvalue distribution of K. The intuition is straightforward: when the model is well grounded, hidden states evolve along a small number of coherent semantic directions, making the spectrum concentrated and the geometric entropy low; when the model is uncertain, the trajectory spreads across more directions, producing a flatter spectrum and higher entropy. The authors argue that this signal lives in a different representational layer from token entropy: one is defined in the unembedding space of next-token probabilities, the other in the hidden-state space of semantic directions. They test additive and multiplicative fusion and find multiplicative fusion consistently stronger, which becomes the final GLU score. The method does not require extra sampling, labels, or architectural changes.da:T512,The evaluation covers three model families and six benchmarks. A central empirical claim is that global geometric uncertainty and local token entropy are nearly orthogonal statistically, which supports the idea that they capture different failure modes rather than redundant views of the same one. In particular, the paper shows that a nontrivial set of wrong answers lies in the low-token-entropy but high-geometric-entropy region, exactly where logit-only confidence methods tend to fail. The main results indicate that multiplicative GLU outperforms either component alone and also beats additive fusion for reliability prediction. The excerpt provided does not include the full metric tables, so it is not possible to quote exact AUROC or calibration gains here with confidence. Still, the paper appears to include meaningful ablations over the choice of local estimator, the choice of geometric entropy formulation, layer selection, and normalization choices. One question to watch closely while reading is whether geometric entropy is merely a proxy for response length or verbosity. The authors claim to normalize for length and to test this explicitly; that point is important because the method is only interesting if it measures semantic drift rather than superficial sequence statistics.db:T436,This is best read as a diagnostic paper, not as a new training recipe. For deeper follow-up, the most interesting questions are whether this signal could be monitored during pretraining, whether it correlates with data quality or optimization instability, and whether it can be used not only for post hoc scoring but also to guide decoding or abstention behavior.dc:T899,The method has two parts. The first measures model-brain correspondence during deductive reasoning. Using task-fMRI data focused on brain regions previously associated with deductive reasoning, the authors extract hidden representations from several open-source LLMs while the models process reasoning problems. They then compute neural predictivity, asking how much explainable variance in the fMRI responses can be accounted for by model representations. Two design choices matter here. One is the separation between aggregate predictivity across all reasoning samples and predictivity within specific reasoning types; the former is much higher than the latter, indicating that the shared structure is coarse rather than mechanism-complete. The other is the use of controls, including untrained models and non-reasoning brain networks, to show that the effect is not a trivial artifact of generic high-dimensional similarity.

The second part uses neural data for intervention. The paper proposes Neural Activation guided Representation Intervention (NARI), an inference-time method, and Neural Activation guided Representation Fine-tuning (NARF), a parameter-update variant. NARI identifies directions in a joint model-brain representational structure that are associated with incorrect responses but can be corrected using neural guidance, then steers intermediate hidden states away from error-prone regions and toward representations associated with correct reasoning. This resembles activation steering, but the steering signal is not derived purely from model-internal statistics; it is constrained by the shared structure between model states and brain activity. NARF pushes the same idea into training by adjusting model parameters so that the model is more likely to form internally correct reasoning representations.

A notable methodological choice is that the authors do not try to regress full fMRI patterns as a global supervision target. Given the noise, limited sample size, and subject variability of fMRI, that would likely overfit irrelevant variance. Instead, they frame the problem as error correction in a shared subspace, which is a more realistic use of the available signal.dd:T5a7,The main findings come in four groups. First, on representation alignment, LLM representations explain about 76% of the explainable variance in aggregate neural responses from deductive-reasoning regions, substantially above untrained-model controls. However, when evaluated within specific reasoning types, predictivity drops to roughly 27%, showing that fine-grained alignment remains limited. Second, the alignment is selective: it is stronger for the reasoning network than for the multiple-demand network or the core language network, supporting the claim that the effect is not reducible to generic language processing. Third, both NARI and NARF can convert a subset of previously incorrect model answers into correct ones, indicating that neural signals are useful not only descriptively but also operationally. One useful experimental lesson is that high global neural predictivity does not automatically imply high reasoning accuracy, whereas localized neural guidance can still improve error cases. The setup is simple: train multiple SAEs on the same activations with identical hyperparameters but different random seeds, choose one run as an anchor, and for each anchor feature match its decoder vector to the most similar decoder vector in each other run using cosine similarity. If the similarity exceeds a threshold, typically 0.7, the feature is counted as having reappeared in that run. Averaging across runs yields a reappearance probability for each feature. This many-to-one matching is much cheaper than one-to-one Hungarian matching, and the paper shows that it produces nearly the same matched feature sets, with IoU 0.978 ± 0.001.

Using this signal, the authors compare stable and unstable features across several axes: reconstruction contribution, marginal predictive utility, activation statistics, token triggers, automatic explanations, and decoder-space geometry. The first major result is a functional asymmetry. Stable features account for most of the reconstruction- and prediction-relevant signal, whereas unstable features tend to have weak marginal impact and are dominated by low-frequency surface-form triggers. The second major result is more subtle: unstable features are often not reproducible as individual latents, but they do recover reproducible lower-rank subspaces. In other words, the basis is unstable while the represented region of activation space is stable.

The paper strengthens this claim with a synthetic experiment where the ground truth is known. Even when the true latent structure is low-rank, SAEs can recover the correct subspace without recovering the same individual latent directions. Finally, the authors build deduplicated feature pools from multiple runs and reconstruct SAEs using stable cross-seed features. In that construction setting, higher explained variance can coincide with higher mean feature probability, suggesting that stability and reconstruction quality do not have to trade off.e0:T5db,The empirical study is broad: multiple models, layers, dictionary sizes, and five SAE variants are included, namely Vanilla ReLU+L1, TopK, BatchTopK, HierarchicalTopK, and JumpReLU. Two quantitative results stand out. First, the proposed many-to-one matching closely agrees with Hungarian matching, with IoU 0.978 ± 0.001, which makes the per-feature stability analysis computationally practical. Second, stable features consistently carry most of the reconstruction and prediction signal, while unstable features contribute much less on the margin. The abstract does not list every number, but the body emphasizes that this pattern is robust across architectures, layers, and SAE variants.

The qualitative analyses are equally important. Automatic explanations and activation statistics show that unstable features are disproportionately associated with low-frequency surface-form triggers rather than semantically or functionally robust abstractions. Decoder-space geometry reveals that these unstable features often cluster into reproducible low-rank regions. The synthetic low-rank experiment confirms that this is not merely an artifact of messy natural-language data: basis non-identifiability with subspace recovery appears even when the ground truth is controlled. Records are generated one by one as JSON with strict validation and regeneration until 10,000 valid samples are collected. Evaluation has three parts: structural reliability via invalid generation rate, statistical fidelity via per-feature TVD between real and synthetic marginals, and memorization risk via DCR ratio plus exact duplication rate. They also track whether the rare fraud base rate is reproduced and inspect how marginal failures propagate into joint structure. The main empirical pattern is that more in-context examples steadily improve numerical fidelity, while categorical fidelity quickly plateaus, especially on high-cardinality long-tail variables. Prompting changes do not fix it. LoRA does, which supports the interpretation that parameter updates can perform the global prior recalibration that ICL cannot.e3:T48b,The experimental signals are consistent across both 7B instruction-tuned models. The real fraud rate is only 0.58%, and the job field has 494 highly imbalanced labels. As the number of in-context examples increases from 1 to 10, numerical features continue to improve, but categorical features hit a clear ceiling. Rare and minority categories are effectively absent from generation. The paper argues that this is not an isolated marginal issue: once categorical marginals are wrong, cross-feature dependencies also degrade. LoRA trained on only 10% or 50% of the real data substantially improves both marginal and joint fidelity, showing that lightweight parameter updates are enough to induce the needed distribution shift. But every LoRA configuration yields a DCR ratio below 1.0, which the authors treat as a warning sign for memorization risk, and exact duplication must be checked alongside it. One of the stronger takeaways is that the ICL failure does not look like a sample-efficiency problem that would vanish with a few more demonstrations. The categorical error stops improving, indicating a structural limit rather than a merely underpowered prompt.e4:T8f0,技术上分成三部分。第一部分是下界构造。作者先在三维欧氏空间里构造一个凸、光滑目标函数 f 和一个非二次但强凸、光滑、条件数受控的 regularizer R。关键点不是把不稳定性归咎于坏条件数，而是利用 mirror map 的非线性，让 primal 空间里很小的初始化差异在 dual 坐标中经过多步更新后持续偏转并累积，最终形成 e^{Ω(ηT)} 的放大。这个构造说明，只要 R 不是二次型，MD 的更新 Jacobian 就可能沿轨迹产生乘法式增长，而二次型 regularizer 对应的线性 dual-primal 映射不会出现这种现象。

第二部分研究负熵 regularizer，也就是 simplex 上最常见的 entropic MD / multiplicative weights。这里作者把机制讲得更直白：负熵在低概率坐标附近的局部曲率很大，等价地说在 ℓ1 几何下高度 ill-conditioned，因此即便目标只是线性的，靠近边界的小扰动也会被指数放大。论文给出了高维下对任意初始化都成立的 lower bound，也覆盖低维 near-boundary 情形；同时还给出 matching 的 exponential upper bound，说明这个量级不是证明技巧造成的松弛，而是 entropic MD 的真实稳定性刻画。作者还把结论推广到更一般的 Legendre regularizer，这使它不只针对负熵一个例子。

第三部分是稳定化方法。Initialization-Anchored MD 在每一步目标里额外加入相对初始化点 x0 的 Bregman 距离，相当于把整个轨迹拴在起点附近。它在 well-conditioned regularizer 下可证明达到 O(ε + 1/√(T log T)) 的初始化稳定性，并保持 O(log T / T) 的优化误差。问题是这个保证依赖 regularizer 在初始化附近的局部 smoothness，遇到 entropy 这类 ill-conditioned 几何时可能失效。于是作者再提出 Fixed-Anchor MD，把 anchor 改成与初始化无关的固定参考点。这样稳定性不再受初始化局部曲率支配，可在 ill-conditioned 情况下给出 O(1/T) 的初始化稳定性，并把优化误差控制在 O(log T / T)。从方法设计上看，这不是简单加 proximal term，而是把“参考模型”从经验技巧提升为稳定性控制变量：anchor 既定义几何，也限制轨迹对初始点的导数增长。e5:T4ea,Its value for pretraining and post-training research is conceptual rather than recipe-driven. It turns a common empirical concern into a formal statement: non-Euclidean geometry can buy useful inductive bias, but it may also degrade robustness to the starting checkpoint. Many RLHF-style and KL-regularized updates can be viewed as mirror-descent-like procedures. If the initialization is the output of upstream pretraining, then downstream instability is not merely noise; it can be an intrinsic property of the algorithm. The contribution has three layers. First, a clean exponential separation between MD and GD in initialization stability. Second, a mechanism-level decomposition: instability can come from non-quadratic geometry itself, even without poor conditioning, and it can also come from the severe local conditioning of entropy near the simplex boundary. Third, two anchored variants of MD that recover stability while preserving optimization guarantees up to logarithmic factors. For researchers working on RL pretraining, continual pretraining, or alignment viewed as optimization, the paper suggests that convergence and reward are not enough; one should also care about the Lipschitz dependence of the training map on the initial checkpoint.e6:T9b3,The technical story has three parts. First, the lower-bound construction in a well-conditioned setting. The authors build a three-dimensional example with a convex smooth objective and a non-quadratic regularizer that is strongly convex, smooth, and well-conditioned in Euclidean norm. The point is to rule out the easy explanation that instability is caused only by bad conditioning. The mechanism is the nonlinearity of the mirror map: a small perturbation in primal space can evolve into a multiplicatively growing discrepancy through repeated dual-space updates and nonlinear primal projection. This cannot happen for quadratic regularizers, where the dual-primal map is linear and the dynamics behave much more like GD.

Second, they analyze entropic mirror descent on the simplex, with negative entropy as the regularizer. Here the mechanism is more transparent. Near low-mass coordinates, negative entropy is highly ill-conditioned in ℓ1 geometry, so even linear objectives can produce exponential amplification of initialization differences. The paper gives a lower bound that is uniform over all simplex initializations in high dimension and also captures the low-dimensional near-boundary regime. It also proves a matching exponential upper bound, which is important because it shows the exponential rate is not a proof artifact but the correct stability scale for entropy MD. The analysis is then extended to broader Legendre regularizers used in online learning and RL.

Third, the stabilization methods. Initialization-Anchored MD adds an extra Bregman penalty to the starting point x0 at every step, effectively tethering the trajectory to the initialization. In well-conditioned settings, this yields initialization stability O(ε + 1/√(T log T)) together with optimization error O(log T / T). But this guarantee depends on local smoothness of the regularizer around the initialization, so it can become vacuous for ill-conditioned geometries such as entropy near the boundary. To address that, the authors introduce Fixed-Anchor MD, where the extra Bregman term is anchored at a fixed reference point independent of the initialization. This removes the dependence on local curvature at the start and gives O(1/T) initialization stability even in ill-conditioned settings, while keeping optimization error at O(log T / T). The design lesson is useful: the reference point is not just a practical heuristic; it can be used as an explicit control knob for stability.e7:T4e1,The paper is theory-first, so the empirical section mainly validates the constructions and the proposed fixes rather than chasing benchmark gains. The numerical results serve two purposes: they show that the lower bounds correspond to observable dynamics, and they compare the two anchored variants against standard MD. In the three-dimensional well-conditioned non-quadratic example, the output discrepancy grows roughly like exp(c·ηT) before saturating at a constant scale, while GD or quadratic regularization does not show this behavior. On the simplex with entropic MD, even linear objectives exhibit the predicted exponential sensitivity, especially near the boundary and in high-dimensional settings. For the stabilization methods, Initialization-Anchored MD suppresses amplification in well-conditioned cases but degrades in entropy geometry when the initialization is close to the boundary; Fixed-Anchor MD remains stable and tracks the theory more closely. The main quantitative takeaways are theoretical rates rather than task metrics: e^{Ω(ηT)} lower bounds for MD sensitivity, O(ε + 1/√(T log T)) stability for Initialization-Anchored MD, O(1/T) for Fixed-Anchor MD, and O(log T / T) optimization error for the anchored variants.e8:T45d,For a skim, focus on three things. Around 45 to 60 minutes is enough to capture the main message; a deeper read should focus on how the dual-primal map creates multiplicative growth along the trajectory.e9:Ta9a,Bergson 的核心设计是把数据归因拆成一条可组合的数据管线，而不是把每种方法写成彼此隔离的脚本。管线大致包括：训练或加载目标模型、收集训练样本梯度、可选的 Hessian/Fisher 近似、梯度归一化与预条件、随机投影压缩、建立磁盘索引、对查询样本做 top-k 影响检索，或者直接在线流式打分。这样的拆法有几个好处。

第一，它统一了 influence-style 方法的实现接口。库里支持 K-FAC、EK-FAC、经验 Fisher、autocorrelation 等 Hessian 近似，也支持 Adam/Adafactor 二阶矩、unit norm 等 normalizer。很多近年的经验发现是，影响函数效果往往不只取决于 Hessian 近似，还强依赖梯度归一化和预条件方式。Bergson 把这些组件显式模块化，方便做 ablation，而不是把方法名当黑盒。

第二，它把存储和查询问题当成一等公民。大模型归因的瓶颈常常不是算一次梯度，而是如何保存、压缩、索引、检索海量 per-example 或 per-token 梯度。Bergson 支持 on-disk gradient store，按模块存储，可选 attention head 级拆分，支持多种精度；查询时可用精确 top-k，也可接 FAISS 做近似最近邻。对于训练集极大、但查询集合固定的场景，作者还提供 on-the-fly scoring：不保存全量梯度库，而是流式扫描训练数据，只累计对预定义 query 的影响分数，以空间换可扩展性。

第三，它覆盖了从近似到精确的训练轨迹归因。论文强调三种此前缺少开源实现的方法：MAGIC、SOURCE、TrackStar。MAGIC 是对完整训练过程做可微分回传，属于精确 unrolled differentiation。作者实现了文献中的 O(N log N) 计算、O(log N) 磁盘 checkpointing 方案，并额外提出一个 O(N) 计算、O(√N) 磁盘的新折中。SOURCE 则是在少量 checkpoint 上重建训练轨迹，做近似 unrolled differentiation。TrackStar 是可扩展 influence approximation，结合经验 Fisher 与优化器状态做归一化。把这三类方法放在同一库里，意味着研究者可以按预算和精度需求选择：想要更准，就走 MAGIC；想要更便宜，就走 influence/TrackStar；想在两者之间折中，就用 SOURCE。

第四，系统层面支持 replicated 和 sharded 并行，目标规模到 405B 参数。这里的意义不是单纯“能跑更大模型”，而是很多归因行为只在大模型上才出现，小模型 proxy 往往失真。库里还强调可复现性和可观测性：每一步产物都序列化，配套 YAML 可重建整条管线，这对归因研究尤其重要，因为不同预处理和近似细节会显著改变结果。ea:T479,Its main contribution is infrastructure. In pretraining work, many questions about data quality, duplication, memorization, and the origins of reasoning eventually reduce to one practical question: which training examples mattered for this behavior? That question is often approximated with lexical overlap or embedding similarity, but the paper explicitly argues that such signals are poor proxies for causal influence. Bergson matters because it puts several major attribution families into one scalable framework: checkpoint-based influence-style methods, approximate multi-checkpoint unrolled differentiation, and exact backpropagation through training via MAGIC. This has two concrete benefits. First, researchers can compare methods under the same model, query set, and data pipeline instead of inheriting incomparable engineering choices. Second, it pushes attribution from a small-scale analysis tool toward something usable in large-model training workflows. For people working on data mixture, filtering, continual pretraining diagnostics, or synthetic data quality, that is more useful than yet another isolated attribution algorithm.eb:Tc5d,The core design choice is to represent attribution as a composable pipeline rather than a collection of disconnected scripts. The pipeline includes training or loading the target model, collecting per-example gradients, optionally applying Hessian or Fisher approximations, normalizing or preconditioning gradients, compressing them with random projections, building an on-disk index, and then either retrieving top-k influential examples for a query or scoring influence on the fly. This decomposition is important for several reasons.

First, it unifies influence-style methods under a common interface. The library supports K-FAC, EK-FAC, empirical Fisher, and autocorrelation-based Hessian approximations, as well as Adam and Adafactor second-moment normalization, unit normalization, and identity variants. In practice, attribution quality often depends not only on the Hessian approximation but also on how gradients are normalized and preconditioned. Bergson exposes these as modular components, which makes ablations and method comparisons much cleaner.

Second, it treats storage and retrieval as first-class problems. For large models, the bottleneck is often not computing a gradient once, but storing, compressing, indexing, and querying massive per-example or per-token gradient collections. Bergson provides on-disk gradient stores organized by module, with optional attention-head splitting and support for multiple precisions. Queries can use exact top-k search or FAISS-based approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval. For cases where the training set is huge but the query set is fixed, the library also supports on-the-fly scoring: instead of materializing a reusable gradient database, it streams through the training data and accumulates influence scores only for predefined queries, trading storage for scalability.

Third, it spans the full accuracy-cost spectrum of trajectory-based attribution. The paper highlights open-source implementations of three methods that previously lacked them: MAGIC, SOURCE, and TrackStar. MAGIC performs exact differentiation through the training process. The implementation includes the checkpointing strategy from prior work with O(N log N) compute and O(log N) disk, and adds a new trade-off with O(N) compute and O(√N) disk. SOURCE reconstructs training from a small number of checkpoints and performs approximate unrolled differentiation. TrackStar is a scalable influence approximation that combines empirical Fisher structure with optimizer-state-based normalization. Putting all three in one library means researchers can choose based on budget and fidelity: MAGIC for higher faithfulness, TrackStar or related influence methods for lower cost, and SOURCE as a middle ground.

Fourth, the systems layer supports both replicated and sharded parallelism, with a stated target scale up to 405B parameters. That matters because many attribution phenomena only become meaningful at large scale; small-model proxies are often misleading. The library also emphasizes reproducibility and observability: each stage emits serialized artifacts and a YAML configuration sufficient to reconstruct the full pipeline.ec:T5ae,This is primarily a systems and tooling paper, so the experiments focus on scalability, method coverage, and case studies rather than a single benchmark score. The authors marginalize over network weights and derive a closed-form posterior over the attention matrix. They then reduce this high-dimensional object to a low-dimensional order-parameter description, with two scalar variables capturing the competition between uniform attention and copy-like attention. This turns training from an opaque parameter-space optimization problem into an analyzable posterior landscape. The central result is that increasing the amount of training data changes which attention pattern dominates the posterior. For softmax attention, the switch is discontinuous and exhibits the hallmarks of a first-order transition, including competing metastable regimes. For linear attention, the copy direction strengthens continuously and then passes through a smoother crossover. The paper also maps these order parameters back to observable loss signatures, explaining the familiar progression from no context use, to in-context unigram statistics, to bigram-level copying. Compared with lazy-limit or frozen-pattern analyses, this work treats the attention pattern itself as the primary degree of freedom and explicitly captures non-Gaussian activations and exact layer coupling.ef:T6fc,The technical contribution is an attention decomposition framework for augmented in-context learning. The prompt is written as x=[I;D;K;q], where I is instruction, D demonstrations, K injected knowledge, and q the query. Attention from query tokens to K is decomposed into a semantic component and a structural component. The structural term is written as λ·σ(K), where σ(K) measures structural intensity and λ is a model-intrinsic sensitivity coefficient that can vary by layer and head.

σ(K) is defined from observable prompt statistics: density of structural delimiters, frequency of relation/slot markers, and repetitiveness of local token patterns. The point is not to claim an exact generative theory of attention, but to provide a testable abstraction: even when semantic content is held fixed, more structured formatting should capture more attention.

The empirical design is built around format-content decoupling. The authors compare semantically equivalent content rendered in different forms, including natural-language passages, relevant triples, irrelevant triples, and noise triples. They also derive a compression-style bound showing that, under normalized attention, increased structural intensity in K must reduce the attention available to D.

The mitigation section proposes five structure-aware strategies, all aimed at reducing λ·σ(K). Two are tested empirically. S3, format flattening, rewrites triples into weaker or more natural language-like forms to reduce delimiter and slot salience. S1, structural dispersal, breaks up highly regular local patterns to reduce repetitive structural cues. Other ideas, such as logit suppression and training-time regularization, are presented more as mathematically motivated directions than fully validated methods.f0:T6ab,The experiments use two model families, Mistral-7B and LLaMA-3-8B, across three QA tasks. Four results matter most.

First, KG triples capture substantially more attention than neutral natural-language text. The paper reports representative structural intensity estimates around 0.70 for KG-formatted content versus about 0.25 for neutral text, and triples absorb roughly 2x to 3x more attention per token.

Second, this attention capture is largely insensitive to semantic relevance. Relevant triples, irrelevant triples, and even noise triples show very similar attention patterns. That is the central empirical support for the paper’s claim: the tax is driven by format before usefulness is even considered.

Third, demonstration attention is compressed by as much as 42% in some settings. So the effect is not a small local preference; it changes the competitive allocation of context budget inside the prompt and can alter ICL behavior.

Fourth, source alignment dominates gating sophistication. On HotpotQA, task-matched BM25 retrieval outperforms mismatched ConceptNet retrieval by more than 30 percentage points, while more elaborate gating contributes no more than about 2 points. The intended message is that choosing the right knowledge source matters far more than adding control logic on top of a poorly matched source.

For mitigation, S3 format flattening is the strongest result: it improves accuracy and reduces attention concentration on structured regions. S1 structural dispersal is mixed and model-dependent, suggesting that reducing structural regularity does not automatically translate into better task performance, possibly because it also harms readability or local parseability.f1:T4bf,For a skim, focus on three parts.
